level.adwa_1896.fact: In 1893 Menelik repudiated the treaty and raised a huge army — by various estimates around 100,000 men, well armed, including with rifles bought in Europe. Taytu joined the campaign and commanded her own force. Baratieri, with some 17–18 thousand soldiers, stood near Adwa and considered retreating for lack of supplies, but Crispi kept sending telegrams about «military phthisis» and demanding action. On the night before 1 March 1896, four Italian brigades moved into the mountains, lost contact with one another, and the Ethiopian army defeated them one by one. About 6–7 thousand Italian and Eritrean soldiers were killed and thousands taken prisoner; Ethiopian losses were heavy too. Crispi resigned, and under the Treaty of Addis Ababa Italy recognized Ethiopia's independence. Adwa became a worldwide symbol of African resistance to colonialism.
level.adwa_1896.goal: Menelik II and Taytu reject the Italian protectorate, Crispi demands a victory — and at Adwa Ethiopia defeats the Italian army
level.adwa_1896.hint: The quarrel starts with a translation. Rome drives the general into battle, and patience in camp won't produce a battle.
level.adwa_1896.intro: 1889. Ethiopia's new emperor, Menelik II, signs a treaty with Italy at Wuchale. A year later it emerges that Article 17 reads differently in the two texts: in Amharic, Ethiopia may conduct its dealings with the European powers through Italy; in Italian, it must — which makes it a protectorate. Empress Taytu, one of the most powerful figures at court, opposes any concession. In Rome, Prime Minister Francesco Crispi expects a resounding victory from General Oreste Baratieri's colonial army.
level.adwa_1896.source: Treaty of Wuchale (2 May 1889, Italian and Amharic texts); Oreste Baratieri, «Memorie d'Africa» (1898); Harold Marcus, «The Life and Times of Menelik II» (1975)
level.adwa_1896.title: Adwa
level.bava_1898.fact: On 7 May a state of siege was declared in Milan and the city was handed over to General Fiorenzo Bava Beccaris. Troops fired rifles and cannon at crowds and barricades; officially about 80 people died, while the opposition put the toll at over a hundred. They even shelled a Capuchin monastery where beggars were queuing at the gate for soup. The socialist Filippo Turati, who had urged people not to rise to provocation, was arrested and sentenced to twelve years (he was amnestied a year later). King Umberto I awarded the general the Grand Officer's Cross of the Military Order of Savoy. In 1900 the anarchist Gaetano Bresci, who had come from the United States, shot the king dead at Monza — in revenge for Milan, as he put it. After that Italy turned onto the path of reform of the Giolitti era.
level.bava_1898.goal: General Bava Beccaris meets a bread riot in Milan with artillery, the socialist Turati is jailed, and the king decorates the general
level.bava_1898.hint: First the city is handed to the army, then come the shots, then the medal. Turati never called for barricades — they jailed him anyway.
level.bava_1898.intro: May 1898. A poor harvest and the Spanish–American War have driven up grain prices, and bread costs almost twice as much. Hunger riots sweep across Italy. In Milan, workers take to the streets after agitators are arrested. The government of the Marquis Antonio di Rudinì fears this is the start of a revolution.
level.bava_1898.source: Records of the Milan military tribunal (1898); correspondence of Filippo Turati and Anna Kuliscioff; Christopher Duggan, «The Force of Destiny» (2007)
level.bava_1898.title: Bava Beccaris's Cannons
level.beccaria_1764.fact: The subject was suggested by Pietro Verri, who was studying the history of torture in Milan at the time. Beccaria wrote slowly and reluctantly, while Pietro's brother Alessandro, who held an office for the care of prisoners, copied out and corrected his pages. In 1764 «On Crimes and Punishments» (Dei delitti e delle pene) appeared anonymously in Livorno. Beccaria argued that torture punishes the innocent before any verdict, that punishment must be proportionate and certain, and that the death penalty is useless. The book was translated into French with a commentary by Voltaire, it inspired Catherine II and the American founders, and in 1766 Rome put it on the Index of Forbidden Books. Beccaria did not «abolish the death penalty single-handedly»: the first state to abolish it was the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, in 1786. In 1768 he himself received a chair in Milan and became an official of the Habsburg reforms. His grandson was the writer Alessandro Manzoni.
level.beccaria_1764.goal: Friends from the «Academy of Fists» push a shy marquis into writing a book against torture and the death penalty — it comes out without his name and sweeps across Europe
level.beccaria_1764.hint: The book isn't written alone. An author's name on the cover in 1764 is not an honour but a risk.
level.beccaria_1764.intro: Milan, the 1760s. Lombardy is ruled by Maria Theresa's Austria. Young noblemen gather at Pietro Verri's in a circle with the provocative name «Academy of Fists» and argue about taxes, trade and laws. The shyest of them is the twenty-five-year-old Marquis Cesare Beccaria, whose own father once kept him under house arrest over a marriage he disapproved of.
level.beccaria_1764.source: Cesare Beccaria, «Dei delitti e delle pene» (Livorno, 1764); correspondence of Pietro and Alessandro Verri
level.beccaria_1764.title: Against Torture
level.brigands_1861.fact: Brigantaggio was neither mere banditry nor a pure people's war. The bands drew in the poor, draft dodgers and former Bourbon soldiers, along with ordinary robbers. The Catalan general José Borjes came on behalf of Francis II and fought alongside Crocco, but the two did not get along; in December 1861 Borjes was shot near Tagliacozzo. The army responded harshly: in 1861 General Enrico Cialdini, the king's lieutenant in Naples, ordered the villages of Pontelandolfo and Casalduni burned. In 1863 the Pica Law introduced military courts in the South for «brigands» and their accomplices. More than a hundred thousand soldiers were sent south; thousands of people were killed, shot or deported. Crocco fled to the Papal States, was handed over and sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted to life at hard labour; in prison he wrote his memoirs. The land question in the South was never resolved — one of the causes of mass emigration.
level.brigands_1861.goal: Former soldier Carmine Crocco leads thousands of the discontented into the forests, and the new kingdom's army spends years crushing the South with military courts
level.brigands_1861.hint: Hope of the Bourbons comes from Rome, and the new state never handed out the land. Crocco must be taken alive — he was put on trial.
level.brigands_1861.intro: 1861. The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies has fallen and the South has become part of Italy. But the new rulers have brought not land but years of conscription, new taxes and unfamiliar officials from Turin. The deposed King Francis II, from Rome, is looking for men to raise the South. In the forests of Basilicata, a former Bourbon soldier and escaped convict, Carmine Crocco, is gathering bands.
level.brigands_1861.source: Pica Law (15 August 1863); report of the Massari parliamentary commission (1863); Carmine Crocco, «Come divenni brigante» (memoirs)
level.brigands_1861.title: The South and the Brigands
level.canossa_1077.fact: Henry got there first. In a bitter winter he crossed the Alps over the Mont Cenis with his wife and little son — the queen was lowered down the icy pass on ox hides. The pope took refuge at Canossa castle with his ally, Margravine Matilda of Tuscany. From 25 to 27 January 1077, by Gregory's own account, the king stood at the gate in a penitent's woollen shirt, barefoot in the snow. Matilda and Abbot Hugh of Cluny, Henry's godfather, persuaded the pope, and on 28 January the excommunication was lifted. «Going to Canossa» became a byword for forced humiliation. But Canossa was no final victory for the pope: in 1080 Gregory excommunicated Henry again, in 1084 the king took Rome, and the exiled pope died in Salerno among the Normans. The Investiture Controversy ended in a compromise only in 1122.
level.canossa_1077.goal: The excommunicated King Henry IV crosses the Alps in winter and stands barefoot at the gate of Canossa for three days, until Matilda and Abbot Hugh persuade the pope
level.canossa_1077.hint: The pope can't be beaten with a sword — you need the road of penance and intercessors. And you must get there before the pope leaves to judge the king before the princes.
level.canossa_1077.intro: 1076. King Henry IV of Germany and Pope Gregory VII are quarrelling over who appoints bishops. At a synod in Worms the king's bishops declared the pope deposed: «Descend, descend!» Gregory replied with excommunication and released Henry's subjects from their oaths. The German princes gave the king a year: if he does not win forgiveness, they will elect another. The pope is setting out for their assembly in Augsburg.
level.canossa_1077.source: Gregory VII, letter to the German princes (January 1077, «Register» IV, 12); Lampert of Hersfeld, «Annals»; Donizo, «Life of Matilda»
level.canossa_1077.title: Canossa
level.caporetto_1917.fact: On 24 October 1917, after a gas attack and a short, powerful bombardment, German and Austrian assault groups advanced not head-on but along the valleys, bypassing the heights. The Second Army's front at Caporetto (today Kobarid in Slovenia) collapsed, and the army retreated more than a hundred kilometres. About 11,000 dead, about 30,000 wounded, some 265–300 thousand taken prisoner. In his bulletin Cadorna blamed the Second Army for cowardice, though the causes lay in the enemy's new tactics, staff errors, poor communications and soldiers' exhaustion. On 9 November he was replaced by Armando Diaz, who improved supplies, granted leave and limited pointless attacks. The Tagliamento could not be held, but on the Piave and Monte Grappa the front stood firm. The government commission of inquiry into Caporetto placed the main responsibility on the high command in its 1919 report. In Italian, «Caporetto» has become a synonym for disaster.
level.caporetto_1917.goal: An Austro-German breakthrough at Caporetto collapses the front, Diaz replaces Cadorna — and the same soldiers stop the enemy on the Piave
level.caporetto_1917.hint: First the breakthrough, then the change of command. The army was stopped not on the Tagliamento — and not by «cowards».
level.caporetto_1917.intro: October 1917. For two and a half years the Italian army has been storming the mountains on the Isonzo — eleven battles, hundreds of thousands dead. Commander-in-chief Luigi Cadorna rules harshly: executions for retreating, generals dismissed. Russia is leaving the war, and Germany is moving divisions to Italy under General Otto von Below. Alongside them stand the Austro-Hungarian armies of Field Marshal Svetozar Boroević.
level.caporetto_1917.source: Report of the Caporetto commission of inquiry (1919); Mark Thompson, «The White War» (2008)
level.caporetto_1917.title: Caporetto
level.carbonari_1820.fact: In July 1820 officers raised the garrison at Nola, General Guglielmo Pepe led troops into Naples, and King Ferdinand swore to the constitution — «sincerely», as tradition has it, with his hand on the Gospels. In early 1821 he went to the Congress of Laibach and asked the powers for help; in March an Austrian army defeated Pepe near Rieti and entered Naples. That same March constitutionalists rose in Piedmont, King Victor Emmanuel I abdicated, and the regent Charles Albert proclaimed the Spanish constitution. But the new king, Charles Felix, ordered him to submit; Charles Albert left, and on 8 April the rebels were defeated at Novara. Santarosa went into exile and died in 1825 fighting for Greek independence. Pepe would return to Italy only in 1848. The secret societies had shown their strength, but also their weakness: without the support of the majority and against Austrian bayonets, they could not hold.
level.carbonari_1820.goal: Secret societies win constitutions in Naples and Turin — but the Neapolitan king calls in the Austrians, and Prince Charles Albert disowns the conspirators
level.carbonari_1820.hint: In 1820 a king's oath weighed less than a request made at Laibach. A regent who grants a constitution is not necessarily a regent who will defend it.
level.carbonari_1820.intro: 1820. In Spain, revolution has forced the king to restore the constitution — and Italy is listening. The Neapolitan army is full of Carbonari, the «charcoal burners» — a secret society with rituals, lodges and a dream of a constitution. In Piedmont, young aristocrats led by Santorre di Santarosa pin their hopes on Prince Charles Albert, of a cadet branch of the House of Savoy.
level.carbonari_1820.source: Guglielmo Pepe, «Memorie» (1847); Santorre di Santarosa, «De la révolution piémontaise» (1821)
level.carbonari_1820.title: The Carbonari
level.charles8_1494.fact: Ludovico opened the road to the French, and in September 1494 Charles's army, with field artillery the like of which had never been seen, crossed the Alps. Piero de' Medici, without consulting the Signoria, went to the king and handed him the fortresses of Sarzana, Pietrasanta and Pisa; in Florence he was declared a traitor, the Medici fled, and power in the city passed to Savonarola's supporters. Pope Alexander VI hesitated, but in December let the French through Rome. On 22 February 1495 Charles entered Naples without a fight. Soon a Holy League formed against him — Venice, Milan, the pope, Spain and the emperor — and at Fornovo the king barely fought his way home. But for sixty-five years Italy became the battlefield of France, Spain and the Empire. Guicciardini begins his «History of Italy» with this year, as the year when «the calamities began».
level.charles8_1494.goal: Ludovico il Moro invites the French king, Piero de' Medici hands him fortresses and loses Florence, the pope lets the army pass — and Charles VIII enters Naples without a fight
level.charles8_1494.hint: The king goes where he is invited. Whoever hands over the keys without asking the republic is already an exile. The pope may close the gates — or may not.
level.charles8_1494.intro: 1494. The balance of Lodi has collapsed: Lorenzo the Magnificent is dead, and Ludovico il Moro, who rules Milan in the name of his weak young nephew, fears that Naples will stand up for the rightful duke. King Charles VIII of France, heir to the Angevin claim to Naples, dreams of glory and a crusade. In Florence rules Lorenzo's son — the young and arrogant Piero.
level.charles8_1494.source: Francesco Guicciardini, «Storia d'Italia», Book I; Philippe de Commynes, «Mémoires», Book VII
level.charles8_1494.title: Charles VIII Opens the Italian Wars
level.chioggia_1380.fact: According to a Venetian chronicle, Pietro Doria answered an offer of peace by saying he would first bridle the bronze horses of St Mark's. The people refused to enlist as oarsmen without Pisani, so he was released. Pisani sank barges loaded with stones in the channels — and the Genoese at Chioggia went from besiegers to besieged. The doge himself put to sea with the fleet. On 1 January 1380 Zeno returned with his squadron; Pietro Doria was killed by a Venetian cannonball, and in June 1380 the starving garrison of Chioggia surrendered. Under the Peace of Turin of 1381 neither side got everything, but after Chioggia Genoa began to cede primacy in the East to Venice. This was a struggle between two trading empires — with mercenaries, artillery and debts.
level.chioggia_1380.goal: The Genoese hold Chioggia at Venice's gates, the people demand the release of the disgraced Pisani, he traps the enemy in the lagoon — and the returning Zeno finishes off the besieged
level.chioggia_1380.hint: An admiral can't command from prison — he has to be released first. Trapping the enemy isn't victory yet: you need a second squadron.
level.chioggia_1380.intro: 1379. Venice and Genoa are at war over trade with the East. Pietro Doria's Genoese fleet has seized Chioggia, a small town on the southern edge of the lagoon, a day's journey from San Marco. Venice's best admiral, Vettor Pisani, sits in prison for his defeat at Pola, and Carlo Zeno's squadron is far away, off the coast of the Levant. Doge Andrea Contarini, an old man past seventy, must decide how to save the republic.
level.chioggia_1380.source: Daniele di Chinazzo, «Chronicle of the War of Chioggia»; Peace of Turin, 1381
level.chioggia_1380.title: Chioggia: Venice on the Brink
level.ciompi_1378.fact: In June 1378 Salvestro pushed through laws against the magnates, and unrest gripped the city — the houses of rich families burned. In July the Ciompi, carrying guild banners, seized the Palazzo della Signoria and raised up as gonfalonier the wool-carder Michele di Lando, who, according to the chroniclers, entered the palace barefoot. Three new guilds were created — for dyers, for tailors and for the Ciompi themselves — and some 13,000 poor men gained political rights for the first time. But the radicals wanted more, and on 31 August Michele himself, with the artisans, crushed them; the Ciompi guild was abolished, and by 1382 the oligarchy was back. The Ciompi were not «the first workers' revolution», but a rare case of the medieval urban poor briefly entering government.
level.ciompi_1378.goal: Salvestro de' Medici's reforms shake Florence, the wool-carders burst into the Palace of the Signoria — and the barefoot Michele di Lando creates guilds for the poor
level.ciompi_1378.hint: The uprising starts from above, but its ally at the top is easily frightened by fire. Power means a place in a guild — without one, there is no vote.
level.ciompi_1378.intro: 1378, Florence. The city is ruled by its guilds, but only the masters of the major guilds — cloth merchants, bankers, lawyers — have a vote. Thousands of wool-carders and dyers, the Ciompi, work for the cloth merchants for a pittance, live in debt and are not even allowed a guild of their own. The Gonfalonier of Justice, Salvestro de' Medici, is planning a reform against the old oligarchy.
level.ciompi_1378.source: Marchionne di Coppo Stefani, «Florentine Chronicle»; Niccolò Machiavelli, «Florentine Histories», Book III
level.ciompi_1378.title: The Ciompi Take the Palazzo
level.colapesce.fact: A Sicilian tale tells how a mother, in anger, cursed her son — «May you turn into a fish!» — and Cola grew webbed fingers and gills. The king decided to test him: he threw a golden cup into the Strait of Messina, Cola brought it back and told what he had seen on the seabed: Sicily rests on three columns — at Messina, Pachino and Marsala — and one of them is cracked. The king wanted to know more and threw his crown into the deep. Cola dived and never came back: he stayed below to hold up the cracked column so the island would not sink. They say that whenever Cola shifts the column from one shoulder to the other, Sicily has an earthquake. In other versions Cola dies because of the king's cruelty or simply vanishes into the deep.
level.colapesce.goal: A boy from Messina becomes half fish, dives for the king's cup — and stays beneath the sea forever, holding Sicily on his shoulders
level.colapesce.hint: Without his mother's word, Cola is just a boy. Whoever took the gold or obeyed his mother won't dive a second time.
level.colapesce.intro: Messina, the Middle Ages. The boy Cola spends whole days in the sea and swims better than the dolphins. His mother fears for him. Rumours of the wonder-swimmer reach the king himself — in most versions, Frederick II.
level.colapesce.source: Sicilian folk tale «Colapesce»; Italo Calvino, «Italian Folktales» (1956)
level.colapesce.title: Cola the Fish
level.dogali_1887.fact: On 25 January 1887 Alula's troops attacked Fort Saati but were driven back. The next day a column under Lieutenant Colonel Tommaso De Cristoforis — about 500 men — set out from Massawa to relieve the fort. At Dogali it was surrounded; more than 400 Italians were killed, including their commander. For Ethiopia this was the defence of its border; for Italy, national mourning: in Rome the square in front of the railway station was named the Square of the Five Hundred. Agostino Depretis's government was shaken, but instead of giving up its colonies Italy sent fresh troops and sought an ally against Yohannes — Menelik, ruler of Shewa. Dogali was the first major defeat of Italian colonialism, to be followed by Adwa and Libya.
level.dogali_1887.goal: Italy pushes inland from Massawa into Ethiopia, and Ras Alula, on Emperor Yohannes's orders, destroys an Italian column at Dogali
level.dogali_1887.hint: The frontier is the business of the emperor and his ras. A column is intercepted in the open, not behind a fort's walls.
level.dogali_1887.intro: 1885. Italy, late to the Scramble for Africa, lands at the port of Massawa on the Red Sea. Soon Italian posts push towards the wells of Saati — onto land that Ethiopia considers its own. The northern frontier is held for Emperor Yohannes IV by Ras Alula Engida, one of the country's finest commanders. He demands that the Italians leave.
level.dogali_1887.source: Reports from Massawa to the Italian parliament (1887); Angelo Del Boca, «Gli italiani in Africa Orientale» (1976)
level.dogali_1887.title: Dogali
level.emigration_1901.fact: FIAT was founded in Turin in 1899; around Turin, Milan and Genoa an «industrial triangle» grew up. At the same time mass emigration was under way: between 1876 and 1914 about 14 million people left Italy, the most in 1913 — some 870,000 in a single year. People did not leave out of idleness, nor did «everyone leave for good»: families sent money home, many came back, and some crossed the ocean for seasonal work. The law of 31 January 1901 created the General Commissariat of Emigration (Bodio became its first commissioner), introduced licences for carriers, inspection of ships and assistance in ports. From 1889 Frances Cabrini worked among the Italians of New York and founded dozens of schools, orphanages and hospitals; in 1946 she was canonized — the first US citizen to become a saint.
level.emigration_1901.goal: FIAT opens in the North while millions leave the South for overseas — a new law protects the emigrants, and in New York Frances Cabrini is there to meet them
level.emigration_1901.hint: The North builds factories, the South emigrates — it is one country. A family is protected by the law, not by the recruiter.
level.emigration_1901.intro: The turn of the 19th and 20th centuries. In Turin, former cavalry officer Giovanni Agnelli and his partners set up a car factory — the North is becoming industrial. Meanwhile whole families are leaving the villages of the South, the Veneto and Friuli for New York, Buenos Aires and São Paulo. Their tickets are sold by recruiting agents, often by deceit. The statistician Luigi Bodio has long been counting this flow and demands that the state take it under its protection.
level.emigration_1901.source: Emigration Law No. 23 (31 January 1901); Donna Gabaccia, «Italy's Many Diasporas» (2000)
level.emigration_1901.title: The Factory and a Ticket to America
level.fasci_1893.fact: In the summer of 1893 the peasants of Corleone won new tenancy contracts — the «Pacts of Corleone» (Patti di Corleone). Giolitti did not want to crush the movement by force, but in November his government fell over the Banca Romana scandal. The new prime minister, the Sicilian Francesco Crispi, saw the Fasci as a conspiracy and a threat to national unity. In January 1894 he declared a state of siege on the island: the leagues were disbanded, thousands were arrested, and military courts sentenced Barbato and Verro to twelve years in prison. Dozens of peasants died in clashes with troops. In 1896 the convicted were amnestied. Verro later became mayor of Corleone and in 1915 was murdered by the Mafia.
level.fasci_1893.goal: Sicily's peasant leagues demand fair contracts; Giolitti won't open fire, but he falls, and Crispi declares a state of siege
level.fasci_1893.hint: Fasci means «leagues», not fascism. Giolitti didn't send troops — a banking scandal brought him down.
level.fasci_1893.intro: 1893. Across Sicily the Fasci dei lavoratori — «workers' leagues» — are growing: farmhands, tenants, sulphur miners. The word fascio simply means «bundle, league»; it has nothing to do with 20th-century fascism. In Piana dei Greci they are led by the doctor Nicola Barbato, in Corleone by Bernardino Verro. They demand new tenancy contracts, lower taxes and the abolition of duties on flour. In Rome, Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti believes the state should stay neutral in labour disputes.
level.fasci_1893.source: Records of the trial of the Fasci Central Committee (Palermo, 1894); Francesco Renda, «I Fasci siciliani» (1977)
level.fasci_1893.title: The Sicilian Fasci
level.five_days_1848.fact: On 18 March a crowd seized the governor's palace, and the «Five Days» began. The Milanese built some 1,700 barricades, boys carried messages by balloon, and the student Luciano Manara led bands to storm the city gates. Cattaneo set up a war council and rejected the truce Radetzky proposed: it would have given the Austrians time. On 22 March Radetzky abandoned the city and fell back to the fortresses of the «Quadrilateral» — Verona, Mantua, Peschiera and Legnago. About 350 Milanese were killed. But this was not «all Italy against Austria»: the moderates called on the Piedmontese king Charles Albert for help, which the republicans did not want. In the summer Radetzky defeated the Piedmontese at Custoza and returned to Milan. Manara was killed in 1849 defending the Roman Republic.
level.five_days_1848.goal: The Milanese build barricades, Cattaneo refuses a truce and unites the bands — and on the fifth day Marshal Radetzky leads his army out of the city
level.five_days_1848.hint: Barricades hold the city, but victory goes to whoever denies the marshal a respite.
level.five_days_1848.intro: March 1848. Revolution is sweeping Europe; on 17 March news of the uprising in Vienna reaches Milan. Lombardy is ruled by Austria, and the garrison is commanded by the eighty-year-old Marshal Joseph Radetzky — 14,000 soldiers, cannon, a fortress in the heart of the city. The Milanese nobility, led by the podestà (mayor) Gabrio Casati, wants reforms and negotiations. The republican, scholar and economist Carlo Cattaneo wants freedom and war to the end.
level.five_days_1848.source: Carlo Cattaneo, «Dell'insurrezione di Milano nel 1848 e della successiva guerra» (1849)
level.five_days_1848.title: The Five Days of Milan
level.florence_1530.fact: In February 1530 in Bologna, Clement VII crowned Charles V with the imperial crown — the last time a pope crowned an emperor; the price was help against Florence. The siege lasted ten months and the city starved. On 3 August at Gavinana, Ferruccio's relief force was defeated; the wounded Ferruccio was finished off by the condottiere Fabrizio Maramaldo. According to tradition, Ferruccio managed to say: «Coward, you are killing a dead man.» Malatesta Baglioni, seeing the situation was hopeless and having come to terms with the enemy, turned his guns on his own side, and on 12 August the city surrendered. The Medici returned, now as hereditary dukes: first Alessandro, then Cosimo I, Grand Duke of Tuscany. The Florentine Republic was over.
level.florence_1530.goal: The Medici pope buys an alliance with the emperor, Ferruccio falls at Gavinana — and a hired commander surrenders Florence, and with it the last republic
level.florence_1530.hint: The siege begins with an alliance of two rulers. The city is surrendered not by the enemy but by the man paid to defend it — unless an oath binds him.
level.florence_1530.intro: 1529. After the Sack of Rome the Florentines once again drove out the Medici and declared a republic — the last in their history; Michelangelo built its fortifications. But Pope Clement VII, himself a Medici, made peace with Emperor Charles V. The emperor's army is besieging Florence, while in the mountains the republic's commissioner Francesco Ferruccio is gathering a force. The city is defended by the hired condottiere Malatesta Baglioni.
level.florence_1530.source: Benedetto Varchi, «Storia fiorentina»; Francesco Guicciardini, «Storia d'Italia», Books XIX–XX
level.florence_1530.title: The Last Florentine Republic
level.galgano.fact: According to his Life, the Archangel Michael appeared to Galgano in a dream and called him to follow. His mother and kin nonetheless persuaded him to ride to his bride, but on the way his horse stopped dead and would not move, then turned of its own accord towards the hill of Montesiepi. There Galgano heard a voice bidding him give up worldly life. He replied that this would be as easy as splitting a stone, struck the rock with his sword — and the blade sank in up to the hilt, leaving the hilt and crossguard above the ground in the shape of a cross. Galgano lived as a hermit for a year and died in 1181; by 1185 he had already been declared a saint. The sword in the stone is still shown in the round chapel of Montesiepi, next to the ruins of the Abbey of San Galgano.
level.galgano.goal: The wild knight Galgano hears the archangel's call, his horse refuses to carry him to his bride — and he thrusts his sword into the rock to become a hermit
level.galgano.hint: First the call, then the road, and only at the end — the stone. Whoever has given his word to his mother or his bride will never become a hermit.
level.galgano.intro: Tuscany, the 12th century. Galgano Guidotti of Chiusdino is a young knight, a reveller and a brawler. His mother, the widow Dionisia, dreams of marrying him off, and his bride Polissena is already waiting. But the knight dreams of the Archangel Michael.
level.galgano.source: Life of Saint Galgano (records of the 1185 canonization inquiry); «Acta Sanctorum»
level.galgano.title: The Sword in the Stone
level.ghetto_1516.fact: On 29 March 1516 the Senate decreed that all the Jews of Venice must live in the Ghetto Nuovo — a quarter on an island where a foundry had once stood (geto means «casting»). The gates were locked from sunset to dawn, the community itself had to pay for its Christian guards, and a yellow badge had to be worn in the streets. This was forced segregation — and at the same time not expulsion: the community stayed in the city, bargained through a condotta for the right to keep loan banks, deal in second-hand goods and practise medicine, built Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Levantine synagogues, and printed books. The word «ghetto» spread from Venice across Europe: in 1555 Pope Paul IV created a ghetto in Rome. The Venetian ghetto was opened only under Napoleon, in 1797.
level.ghetto_1516.goal: The Venetian Senate does not expel the Jewish community but locks it in on the island of the Ghetto Nuovo — and the community bargains over the terms on which it will live behind gates
level.ghetto_1516.hint: Expulsion was also a historical option, but Venice chose otherwise. The terms of life in the ghetto are not granted — they are bargained for.
level.ghetto_1516.intro: 1516, Venice. The republic is at war, the treasury is empty, and refugees from the mainland — among them hundreds of Jews — have filled the city. Jewish bankers lend to the state and to the poor, but preachers demand that the «infidels» be expelled, and many patricians are uneasy at having them close by. The community's leader, Anselmo del Banco, negotiates with the Senate, and the chronicler Marino Sanudo records every word.
level.ghetto_1516.source: Marino Sanudo, «I Diarii», vol. XXII; decree of the Venetian Senate of 29 March 1516
level.ghetto_1516.title: The Venetian Ghetto
level.guarantees_1871.fact: On 13 May 1871 parliament passed the Law of Guarantees: the pope was declared inviolable, kept the Vatican and the Lateran and the right to receive ambassadors, and was to receive an annual allowance of 3.2 million lire from the state. On 15 May Pius IX answered with the encyclical «Ubi nos»: the law was a one-sided act of the state that had seized Rome; he did not recognize it and would not take the money. The pope never again left the Vatican and called himself its prisoner; Catholics were soon forbidden to take part in parliamentary elections (Non expedit, made final in 1874). On 1 July 1871 the capital officially moved from Florence to Rome. The «Roman Question» remained open until the Lateran Pacts of 1929.
level.guarantees_1871.goal: Italy makes Rome its capital and offers the pope guarantees, but Pius IX rejects them and declares himself a prisoner in the Vatican
level.guarantees_1871.hint: You can only reject what has been offered. The pope neither leaves nor makes peace — the dispute will drag on for sixty years.
level.guarantees_1871.intro: 1871. Italian troops have entered Rome through the breach at Porta Pia, and papal rule over the city is over. Now Prime Minister Giovanni Lanza's government must decide what becomes of the pope, who remains head of the Church for Catholics all over the world. Finance Minister Quintino Sella insists that the capital of the new Italy can only be Rome.
level.guarantees_1871.source: Law of Guarantees (13 May 1871); Pius IX, encyclical «Ubi nos» (15 May 1871)
level.guarantees_1871.title: Prisoner of the Vatican
level.intervention_1915.fact: On 26 April 1915 Sonnino secretly signed a treaty in London: Italy would enter the war within a month and would receive Trentino, South Tyrol, Trieste, Istria and part of Dalmatia. Parliament knew nothing of it. When more than three hundred deputies left their visiting cards at Giolitti's as a sign of support for neutrality, Salandra resigned. King Victor Emmanuel III sent for Giolitti, but Giolitti declined to form a government, and the king refused the resignation. Interventionist rallies filled the squares — the «Radiant May» — and among the speakers was the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio. On 20 May the Chamber granted the government full powers, and on 23 May Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary. The country went to war divided: interventionists, neutralists, socialists and Catholics all saw it differently.
level.intervention_1915.goal: A secret Treaty of London, the king's refusal to let Salandra go, and the «Radiant May» — Italy enters the war against the will of the Chamber's majority
level.intervention_1915.hint: First the treaty, then the king, then the Chamber. Vienna offered concessions too, and the king could have sent for a neutralist.
level.intervention_1915.intro: 1914. Italy is a member of the Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary, but the alliance is defensive, and Austria attacked Serbia on its own. Italy declares neutrality. In the spring of 1915 both sides bargain for her. Vienna is ready to give up part of Trentino. The Entente promises more. Prime Minister Antonio Salandra and Foreign Minister Sidney Sonnino speak of «sacred egoism». And former Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti, who has the majority of deputies behind him, believes that «quite a lot» can be gained without war.
level.intervention_1915.source: Treaty of London (26 April 1915); record of the Chamber of Deputies sitting of 20 May 1915; Antonio Salandra, «L'intervento (1915)» (1930)
level.intervention_1915.title: Neutrality Breaks
level.kingdom_1805.fact: On 26 May 1805 in Milan Cathedral, Napoleon placed the Iron Crown of the Lombard kings on his own head with the words «God has given it to me — woe to him who touches it.» The emperor's twenty-three-year-old stepson Eugène de Beauharnais became viceroy, while Melzi was sidelined — in 1807 he was given the title of Duke of Lodi. The Kingdom of Italy (Lombardy, the Veneto, part of Emilia and the Marche) received the Napoleonic Code, prefects, a unified administration, an army and a tricolour flag — green, white and red. But it paid dearly: Finance Minister Giuseppe Prina collected taxes and recruits, and tens of thousands of Italian soldiers died in Spain and Russia. When the empire collapsed, in April 1814, a Milanese mob lynched Prina. Many future figures of the Risorgimento came from the officials and officers of Napoleonic Italy.
level.kingdom_1805.goal: Napoleon turns the Italian Republic into a kingdom, crowns himself with the Iron Crown, makes his stepson viceroy — and Minister Prina collects taxes and recruits
level.kingdom_1805.hint: First the crown, then the viceroy, then the money. Melzi's republic is a fine option that Napoleon did not choose.
level.kingdom_1805.intro: 1805. Napoleon is already Emperor of the French, and in Milan there is an Italian Republic — he himself is its president, but it is actually run by the vice-president, the Milanese aristocrat Francesco Melzi d'Eril. Melzi dreams of genuine Italian autonomy. But the emperor decides otherwise: the republic is to become a kingdom, and the crown was first offered to his brother Joseph, who declined.
level.kingdom_1805.source: Statuto costituzionale del Regno d'Italia (1805); Francesco Melzi d'Eril, «Memorie, documenti e lettere inedite» (1865)
level.kingdom_1805.title: The Kingdom of Italy
level.legnano_1176.fact: In the spring of 1176 at Chiavenna, Barbarossa asked for help from his powerful cousin Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria; according to a later tradition he even fell on his knees before him, but Henry refused. On 29 May at Legnano the imperial knights crushed the League's cavalry and reached the carroccio — the wagon bearing the standard and an altar, around which the Milanese infantry stood. The infantry held, the cavalry returned with reinforcements, and the emperor, unhorsed, barely escaped. In 1177 in Venice Barbarossa made peace with Alexander III, and the Peace of Constance of 1183 recognized the cities' self-government. Alberto da Giussano and his «Company of Death» are a later legend, especially beloved in the age of the Risorgimento.
level.legnano_1176.goal: The Lombard cities unite in a league with the pope's blessing, Henry the Lion leaves the emperor without reinforcements — and at Legnano Barbarossa's knights flee before the townsmen's infantry
level.legnano_1176.hint: A city that has paid the emperor won't join the alliance. A strong emperor is beaten when he is left without help.
level.legnano_1176.intro: 1176. For twenty years Emperor Frederick Barbarossa has been trying to bring the Italian cities back under imperial rule: he demands taxes, installs his own podestàs, and in 1162 razed Milan to the ground. The cities — Milan, Cremona, Verona, Padua — have united in the Lombard League, backed by Pope Alexander III, whom the emperor does not recognize. Barbarossa needs fresh troops from Germany.
level.legnano_1176.source: Annales Mediolanenses (Milanese Annals); Romuald of Salerno, «Chronicle»; Peace of Constance, 1183
level.legnano_1176.title: Legnano: The Cities against Barbarossa
level.libya_1911.fact: On 29 September 1911 Italy declared war, and in October it occupied Tripoli and the ports. It was no stroll: on 23 October at Shar al-Shatt Ottoman and Arab fighters struck the Italian positions, after which came executions and deportations of civilians. On 1 November Lieutenant Giulio Gavotti dropped grenades from an aeroplane onto an oasis — the first aerial bombing in history. A young officer, Enver Bey, made his way into Cyrenaica and organized resistance together with the Senussi. On 18 October 1912, under the Peace of Ouchy, the Ottoman Empire, which was then entering the Balkan War, ceded the provinces. But for the local people the war was not over: the Senussi fought on, and the sheikh and teacher Omar al-Mukhtar later became the main leader of resistance in Cyrenaica — especially in the 1920s, until his capture and execution in 1931.
level.libya_1911.goal: Italy takes Libya from the Ottoman Empire, but peace with the Porte does not end the war: Senussi resistance goes on
level.libya_1911.hint: Resistance is organized while Ottoman officers are still in the desert. Peace with the Porte is not peace with Libya.
level.libya_1911.intro: September 1911. France already controlled Tunisia and was tightening its grip on Morocco; Britain held Egypt. In Rome, Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti and Foreign Minister Antonino di San Giuliano decide that the last Ottoman province in North Africa — Tripolitania and Cyrenaica — must become Italian. The press promises «a stroll». But the desert is home to Arab and Berber tribes, and the Senussi order is a power to be reckoned with from the oases to the Sahara.
level.libya_1911.source: Treaty of Ouchy (18 October 1912); Giovanni Giolitti, «Memorie della mia vita» (1922); Angelo Del Boca, «Gli italiani in Libia» (1986)
level.libya_1911.title: The Libyan War
level.lodi_1454.fact: Cosimo broke with Venice and backed Sforza with money. The war dragged on for several more years; Sforza even called in a French prince, René of Anjou, but he soon left. In May 1453 the Turks took Constantinople, and the Italian powers took fright. On 9 April 1454 Milan and Venice signed the Peace of Lodi, and in 1455 Pope Nicholas V sealed the Italic League — an alliance of the five powers for twenty-five years. The «balance» held, with interruptions, until 1494; under it flourished Lorenzo's Florence and Ludovico's Milan. But this was not «the perfect peace of the Renaissance» — it was a fragile balance kept up by spies, ambassadors and mercenaries.
level.lodi_1454.goal: Cosimo de' Medici bets on the new Duke of Milan, Sforza and Venice sign the Peace of Lodi — and Italy's five powers seal it with the Italic League
level.lodi_1454.hint: First money, then peace, then the alliance. Whoever calls in the French won't join a league of Italians.
level.lodi_1454.intro: 1450. The condottiere Francesco Sforza, husband of the last Visconti's daughter, becomes Duke of Milan. Against him stand Doge Francesco Foscari's Venice, which wants Lombardy, and Alfonso of Aragon's Naples. Cosimo de' Medici, until yesterday Venice's ally, must decide where to stake Florentine money. Italy is ruled by five powers — Milan, Venice, Florence, the pope and Naples — and none can defeat the rest.
level.lodi_1454.source: Text of the Peace of Lodi (1454); Niccolò Machiavelli, «Florentine Histories», Book VI; Francesco Guicciardini, «Storia d'Italia», Book I
level.lodi_1454.title: The Peace of Lodi
level.lombards_568.fact: Alboin entered Italy almost unopposed. Paul the Deacon tells how he surveyed the country from a mountain on the border, and put his nephew Gisulf in charge of the first city, Forum Iulii — Gisulf asked to be given the best Lombard clans. So the first duchy, Friuli, came into being. Pavia held out for three years and fell in 572; it later became the capital of the Lombard kingdom. Ravenna, Rome, Naples and the coast remained Constantinople's — for two centuries Italy was divided into Lombard and Byzantine lands. In that same year, 572, Alboin was murdered: at a feast he had forced his wife Rosamund to drink from the skull of her father, the Gepid king, and she conspired with his shield-bearer. Historians regard the story that the Lombards were invited in by the aggrieved Byzantine general Narses as a later legend.
level.lombards_568.goal: King Alboin leads the Lombards into Italy, leaves his nephew as Duke of Friuli, takes Pavia — and Ravenna stays Byzantine
level.lombards_568.hint: First a screen in the mountains, then the cities. Ravenna can't be taken — you'll have to share Italy with it. And don't drink from just anything at a feast.
level.lombards_568.intro: 568. Italy has barely survived Justinian's twenty-year Gothic War, plague and famine. In the spring a whole people crosses the Julian Alps — King Alboin's Lombards, with their families, herds and Saxon allies. In Ravenna sits the Byzantine prefect Longinus.
level.lombards_568.source: Paul the Deacon, «History of the Lombards», Book II, 5–28
level.lombards_568.title: The Lombards Cross the Alps
level.loreto.fact: According to legend, in December 1294 angels set the Holy House down in the laurel grove of the widow Loreta — hence the name Loreto. Robbers ran riot in the grove, so the House flew to the field of two brothers from Recanati; the brothers quarrelled over the pilgrims' gifts, and the House came to rest in the middle of a public road, where it still stands today — inside an enormous basilica. Around 1296, tradition says, the miracle became known through the hermit Paul, who had seen a light over the spot. This is a devotional tradition, not a verifiable event: the oldest written accounts appeared only in the 15th century, and historians propose an earthly version — the stones of the shrine may have been brought by ship at the behest of the Greek Angelos family, who ruled Epirus. Loreto became one of the great pilgrimage sites of Europe, and Our Lady of Loreto the patron saint of aviators.
level.loreto.goal: Angels carry the Virgin Mary's House across the sea to a laurel grove, from there to the brothers' field — and finally onto the road, where a hermit finds it
level.loreto.hint: The House won't stay where it isn't welcome: neither in a grove full of robbers nor with those who squabble over gifts. Look for land that belongs to no one.
level.loreto.intro: The end of the 13th century. Tradition says that angels lifted the house in Nazareth where the Virgin Mary had lived and carried it across the sea — first to the hill of Trsat near present-day Rijeka (the legend calls it Dalmatia), and three years later to the Italian shore, near the town of Recanati.
level.loreto.source: Pietro di Giorgio Tolomei, «Translatio miraculosa ecclesie Beate Virginis Marie de Loreto» (c. 1472)
level.loreto.title: The House That Flew to Loreto
level.melfi_1059.fact: Hildebrand came to terms with Richard of Aversa, who sent a force against the antipope. In August 1059, at the Synod of Melfi, Nicholas II received the Normans' oath: Richard became Prince of Capua, and Robert Guiscard «by the grace of God and Saint Peter Duke of Apulia and Calabria and, with their help, future Duke of Sicily» — still held by the Arabs. The Normans undertook to pay a census and to protect the pope. In the autumn their knights besieged Galeria, where Benedict X had taken refuge, and he surrendered. By disposing of lands it did not own, the papacy acted as a secular player; the Normans went from mercenaries to lawful rulers and built a strong state in the south.
level.melfi_1059.goal: Yesterday's enemies strike a deal: Pope Nicholas II recognizes the Norman leaders as duke and prince, and their knights drive out the antipope
level.melfi_1059.hint: Six years ago the Normans took a pope prisoner — fighting won't help. The alliance begins with an embassy, and the reward with an oath to the pope, not to the emperor.
level.melfi_1059.intro: 1059. The reformers, led by Archdeacon Hildebrand, are being pushed aside by the Roman nobility, who have installed a pope of their own — Benedict X. The reforming Pope Nicholas II needs swords. The Normans of the south have them — Robert Guiscard in Apulia and Richard in Aversa. But in 1053 at Civitate the Normans routed the army of Pope Leo IX and took him prisoner.
level.melfi_1059.source: Amatus of Montecassino, «History of the Normans»; Geoffrey Malaterra, «The Deeds of Count Roger»; William of Apulia, «The Deeds of Robert Guiscard»
level.melfi_1059.title: Melfi: The Pope Recognizes the Normans
level.meloria_1284.fact: On 6 August 1284 the Genoese took up position off Porto Pisano; the Pisan fleet came out to meet them and engaged them by the rocks of Meloria. Zaccaria's squadron held back, and at the height of the battle struck the Pisans in the flank. Pisa lost dozens of galleys, thousands of sailors were killed, and some nine thousand were taken prisoner by Genoa — among them the podestà Morosini. «If you want to see Pisa, go to Genoa», people joked at the time. Ugolino led his galleys away, and in Pisa he was suspected of treachery. He became ruler of the city, but in 1288 his enemies locked him in a tower with his sons and grandsons, and early in 1289 they starved to death; Dante placed him in the ninth circle of the «Inferno». After Meloria Pisa never regained its sea power.
level.meloria_1284.goal: Genoa lures out the Pisan fleet, smashes it with a hidden squadron by the rocks of Meloria and captures the podestà — while Count Ugolino leaves the battle
level.meloria_1284.hint: A fleet driven off at the harbour walls won't lure the enemy out any more. Whoever stands where the prisoner stood in battle ends up a prisoner; Ugolino was not remembered as a captive.
level.meloria_1284.intro: 1284. For two hundred years Genoa and Pisa have been dividing the Tyrrhenian Sea: Corsica, Sardinia, trade with the East. Pisa has made the Venetian Albertino Morosini its podestà; beside him stands Count Ugolino della Gherardesca, a cunning politician from a Ghibelline family who had by then drawn close to the Guelphs. The Genoese fleet is commanded by Oberto Doria and Benedetto Zaccaria — merchant, seaman and owner of alum mines in Asia Minor.
level.meloria_1284.source: Jacopo Doria, continuation of the «Annales Ianuenses»; Dante, «Divine Comedy», «Inferno», Cantos XXXII–XXXIII
level.meloria_1284.title: Meloria
level.naples_1734.fact: In the spring of 1734 the Spanish army under the Count of Montemar marched south. On 10 May Charles made his ceremonial entry into Naples, and on 25 May at Bitonto Montemar routed the imperial troops — for this victory he received the title of Duke of Bitonto. Then Sicily fell. Under the Peace of Vienna of 1738 Charles kept Naples and Sicily but gave Parma to Austria. Naples was once again the capital of an independent kingdom: Charles built the Teatro San Carlo and the palace at Caserta and began the excavations of Herculaneum and Pompeii. In 1759 he left for Madrid as King Charles III of Spain, leaving his son Ferdinand in Naples. In this story the Italian South is no «backward periphery» but one of the largest kingdoms on the peninsula.
level.naples_1734.goal: Elisabeth Farnese sends her son the infante south, Montemar's army defeats the Austrians at Bitonto — and Naples gets a king of its own for the first time in two hundred years
level.naples_1734.hint: The mother wins her son a crown, but only a victory in the field opens the gates. A peace made too early will leave the infante without a throne.
level.naples_1734.intro: 1734, the War of the Polish Succession. For more than two centuries Naples and Sicily have been governed by viceroys — first from Madrid, from 1707 from Vienna. The Spanish queen Elisabeth Farnese, second wife of Philip V, knows that her sons from this marriage will not inherit the Spanish throne. The eldest, the eighteen-year-old Infante Charles, has already received Parma. But his mother wants a real kingdom for him.
level.naples_1734.source: Treaty of Vienna (1738); Giuseppe Galasso, «Il Regno di Napoli. Il Mezzogiorno borbonico e napoleonico (1734–1815)» (2007)
level.naples_1734.title: A King for Naples
level.odoacer_476.fact: On 28 August 476 Odoacer defeated Orestes near Piacenza and executed him. He spared the very young Romulus (by various estimates fourteen to sixteen years old) for his youth and good looks: he gave him a pension of six thousand solidi and sent him to live in the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples. Odoacer did not install a new emperor. The Roman Senate sent the imperial insignia to Zeno in Constantinople, saying that one common emperor was enough for the West. Zeno gave Odoacer the title of patrician, although formally he continued to recognize the exiled emperor Julius Nepos. Odoacer did not destroy Rome: the Senate, the laws and the officials carried on, and he himself ruled as King of Italy. The year 476 is a convenient date for textbooks, but to contemporaries it was just another change of power, not «the end of antiquity».
level.odoacer_476.goal: The federate leader Odoacer defeats Orestes, sends the boy emperor into retirement and returns the regalia to Constantinople: there is no longer an emperor in the West
level.odoacer_476.hint: An emperor doesn't have to be killed — he can be pensioned off. And the purple is more dangerous to keep than to send away.
level.odoacer_476.intro: 476. In Ravenna reigns the boy Romulus Augustulus, put on the throne by his father, the general Orestes. The Germanic mercenaries, the federates, demand a third of the land of Italy, as was the custom in other provinces. Orestes refuses. The soldiers proclaim their commander, the Scirian Odoacer, king.
level.odoacer_476.source: Anonymus Valesianus, Part II; Jordanes, «Getica», 242–243; Marcellinus Comes, «Chronicle»
level.odoacer_476.title: A King without an Emperor
level.otto_962.fact: Adelaide escaped from captivity — through a tunnel, as tradition has it — and asked Otto for help. In 951 he came to Italy, married her at Pavia and took the title of King of Italy. Berengar was allowed to go on ruling as a vassal, but he again began to press his neighbours and the pope. In 961 Pope John XII called on Otto for help, and on 2 February 962 crowned him emperor in Rome; Adelaide was crowned with him. In the «Privilegium Ottonianum» the emperor confirmed the papal possessions but required that each new pope swear an oath to him before consecration. Within a year John XII began intriguing against Otto and was deposed. So began the Holy Roman Empire — and the long dispute between popes and emperors over who stood higher. Italy became part of imperial politics, but not a province «conquered by Germany».
level.otto_962.goal: Queen Adelaide escapes captivity and marries the German king Otto — and eleven years later the pope crowns him emperor in Rome
level.otto_962.hint: The captive must break free on her own — and on no account promise her hand to someone else's son. The one who becomes emperor is the one who is already King of Italy.
level.otto_962.intro: 950. The young King Lothair of Italy has died, and Margrave Berengar of Ivrea has seized the crown. He has locked Lothair's nineteen-year-old widow, Adelaide, in a castle on Lake Garda: let her marry his son, and the throne will stay in the family. Beyond the Alps, the German king Otto watches Italy with interest.
level.otto_962.source: Liutprand of Cremona, «Antapodosis» and «Liber de gestis Ottonis»; Widukind of Corvey, «Deeds of the Saxons»; «Privilegium Ottonianum» (962)
level.otto_962.title: Otto's Crown
level.parthenopean_1799.fact: The French left in May, and the republic was on its own. Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo raised an «Army of the Holy Faith» in Calabria — the Sanfedisti: peasants, priests, former bandits, soldiers. In June they took Naples, and the city was swept by lynchings. Ruffo offered the defenders of the forts an honourable capitulation: their lives and passage to France. But Admiral Nelson, newly arrived, declared it void together with the king and queen. About a hundred republicans were executed — among them Eleonora Pimentel, hanged on 20 August 1799 in the Piazza del Mercato. The historian and eyewitness Vincenzo Cuoco called the republic a «passive revolution»: its ideas never reached the people. This is not a story of «the enlightened against the savages»: the Sanfedisti were driven by faith, loyalty to the king, fear of French requisitions and social revenge, and Nelson's role is still debated.
level.parthenopean_1799.goal: The Neapolitan republicans hold the city for five months, Cardinal Ruffo's army takes it back, and the promise to spare those who surrender is revoked by Nelson and the king
level.parthenopean_1799.hint: The cardinal promises the capitulation, but he is not the one who breaks it. Royal mercy never happened in this story.
level.parthenopean_1799.intro: In December 1798 King Ferdinand fled on a British ship to Palermo, and in January 1799 the French army enters Naples. Neapolitan patriots — lawyers, doctors, priests, aristocrats — proclaim the Parthenopean Republic. Its voice is Eleonora Fonseca Pimentel, a poet of Portuguese descent: her newspaper, the «Monitore Napoletano», explains the revolution to the people. But the lazzaroni — the city's poor — and the provincial peasants side with the king and the Church.
level.parthenopean_1799.source: Vincenzo Cuoco, «Saggio storico sulla rivoluzione napoletana del 1799» (1801); Benedetto Croce, «La rivoluzione napoletana del 1799» (1897)
level.parthenopean_1799.title: The Parthenopean Republic
level.pavia_774.fact: In the summer of 773 Charles offered Desiderius fourteen thousand gold solidi to return the papal cities, but he refused. The Frankish army marched across the Alps; Adelchis's barrier at the Chiuse in the Susa valley held until a Frankish detachment outflanked it along mountain paths — and the Lombards fled. Adelchis escaped to Constantinople and long tried to return. Pavia held out for nine months and surrendered in June 774; Desiderius and his wife were sent to a monastery in Francia. Charles became «King of the Franks and the Lombards», and at Easter 774 in Rome he confirmed Pepin's Donation — the basis of the future Papal States. The Lombard kingdom vanished, but Lombard dukes, laws and families remained, and in the south the Duchy of Benevento lived on for another three centuries.
level.pavia_774.goal: The pope calls on the Franks for help, Charles outflanks the Alpine barrier, takes Pavia after a nine-month siege — and becomes King of the Lombards
level.pavia_774.hint: The Franks come into Italy at the pope's request. The gorge held by the prince can't be taken head-on — it is outflanked. And whoever takes the gold won't fight.
level.pavia_774.intro: 772. The Lombard king Desiderius is seizing from the pope the cities that, sixteen years earlier, the Frankish king Pepin had «given to Saint Peter». King Desiderius and the Lombard army hold the Alpine passes, and his son Adelchis is his father's mainstay. Charles, King of the Franks, has recently sent his wife — Desiderius's daughter — back home. Pope Hadrian I sends envoys to him.
level.pavia_774.source: «Royal Frankish Annals» (773–774); «Liber Pontificalis», Life of Hadrian I; Einhard, «Life of Charlemagne», ch. 6
level.pavia_774.title: Pavia: The Franks Enter Italy
level.plague_1630.fact: The governor did not close the city in time, and in the spring of 1630 the epidemic flared up in earnest. The city authorities asked Cardinal Federico Borromeo to hold a procession with the relics of his cousin, Saint Charles; at first he refused, fearing the crowds, but he gave way — and in June, after the procession, the number of sick rose further. Some 60,000 of the 130,000 inhabitants died. That summer a neighbour, Caterina Rosa, saw from her window the health commissioner Guglielmo Piazza running his hand along a wall, and accused him; under torture he named the barber Gian Giacomo Mora, and both were executed, Mora's house was demolished and a «column of infamy» erected in its place. There were no «anointers»: the plague was spread by fleas and people. Alessandro Manzoni described these events in «The Betrothed» and examined the trial in «The Column of Infamy» as an example of how fear breeds judicial falsehood.
level.plague_1630.goal: The governor brushes off the doctor, a procession with relics spreads the contagion — and the frightened city hunts for «anointers» and executes an innocent man
level.plague_1630.hint: A city closed in time would not have become the Milan of 1630. The cardinal did not agree to the procession at once. The culprit for the epidemic is found not by doctors but by neighbours.
level.plague_1630.intro: 1629. German Landsknechts are marching through Lombardy to the war over Mantua — and bringing the plague with them. The protophysician Alessandro Tadino warns the governor, Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, but the governor is busy besieging Casale. Milan is starving, the lazaretto is overflowing, and townspeople whisper that the contagion is being spread on purpose by «anointers» — untori who smear the walls with poisonous ointment.
level.plague_1630.source: Alessandro Tadino, «Raguaglio» (1648); Giuseppe Ripamonti, «De peste Mediolani» (1641); Alessandro Manzoni, «Storia della colonna infame» (1840)
level.plague_1630.title: Plague and the «Anointers» of Milan
level.pontida.fact: Tradition tells that on 7 April 1167 envoys of the Lombard cities gathered at the Abbey of Pontida and swore loyalty to one another against the emperor; afterwards they helped the Milanese rebuild their city. The knight Alberto da Giussano supposedly formed the «Company of Death» — nine hundred young men sworn to die by the carroccio, the wagon with the standard and an altar, rather than retreat — and in 1176 at Legnano they stood firm against Barbarossa. The Lombard League, its union of cities and the victory at Legnano are real, but the oath at Pontida is mentioned only by late sources, and Alberto da Giussano first appears in the chronicler Galvano Fiamma in the 14th century, a century and a half later. He was made a hero of the Risorgimento in the 19th century: Verdi wrote the opera «La battaglia di Legnano», and a statue of the warrior with his sword stands in Legnano.
level.pontida.goal: The exiles of ruined Milan make peace with their neighbours, the cities swear an oath at Pontida — and Alberto da Giussano raises the Company of Death
level.pontida.hint: An alliance begins with a plea, not with revenge. The oath is sworn together, and the company is needed only once the league exists.
level.pontida.intro: 1167. Five years ago Emperor Frederick Barbarossa took Milan and ordered it razed, and the neighbouring cities — Cremona, Lodi, Pavia — helped him because they hated the Milanese. Now the imperial governors are strangling everyone with taxes. The exiles of Milan are looking for allies.
level.pontida.source: Galvano Fiamma, chronicle (14th century); 12th-century Milanese annals on the Lombard League
level.pontida.title: The Oath of Pontida
level.roger_1130.fact: Anacletus II, backed by Rome but not by most of Europe, needed a strong ally and granted Roger the royal title by a bull. At Christmas 1130 Roger was crowned in Palermo Cathedral. Innocent II was supported by the emperor, France and Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux, who called Roger «the Sicilian tyrant». After Anacletus died (1138), Innocent himself made war on Roger, but in 1139 he was captured at Galluccio — and by the Treaty of Mignano recognized him as king. The Kingdom of Sicily spoke Latin, Greek and Arabic: Greek admirals and Arab scholars served at court, and the geographer al-Idrisi compiled «The Book of Roger» for him. But this was no «tolerant utopia» — it was a multilingual monarchy, strong and harsh.
level.roger_1130.goal: The Norman count Roger receives a crown from the antipope, is crowned in Palermo — and nine years later captures the lawful pope to make him recognize him as king
level.roger_1130.hint: In a papal schism the crown is given by the one who needs an ally. Whoever bows too soon is no longer a king. Recognition is not won by preaching.
level.roger_1130.intro: 1130. The Normans, who came to southern Italy as mercenaries, have in a hundred years brought Sicily, Calabria and Apulia under one hand. Count Roger II rules from Palermo — a city of mosques, Greek churches and Latin cathedrals. All he lacks is the title of king. And in Rome there happens to be a schism: the cardinals have elected two popes — Innocent II and Anacletus II.
level.roger_1130.source: Falco of Benevento, «Chronicle»; Romuald of Salerno, «Chronicle»; Alexander of Telese, «The Deeds of King Roger»
level.roger_1130.title: Roger's Crown
level.roman_republic_1849.fact: From Gaeta the pope called on the Catholic powers to restore his rule. The first to respond was France under President Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, who needed the support of French Catholics: in April General Oudinot's corps landed at Civitavecchia. The republicans beat off the first assault on 30 April; then came the negotiations of the diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, which Paris disavowed. In June the French laid siege to the city, and for almost a month Garibaldi, with volunteers from all over Italy, held the Janiculum hill; Luciano Manara was killed there, and the poet Goffredo Mameli, author of the future Italian anthem, was wounded and died of infection in July. On 3 July the French entered Rome. That same day the republic solemnly proclaimed its constitution — one of the most radical of its time: abolition of the death penalty, freedom of worship, universal male suffrage. Garibaldi left the city with his men; during the retreat his wife Anita died. This was a dispute not between «faith and godlessness» but over the pope's temporal power, the constitution and international politics; French troops protected papal rule in Rome until 1870 — with a break in 1866–1867.
level.roman_republic_1849.goal: The pope flees to Gaeta, Rome becomes Mazzini's republic, Garibaldi defends the city for a month — but a French corps returns Rome to the pope
level.roman_republic_1849.hint: Rome is not surrendered without a fight — but it is not held either: the troops come at a call from Gaeta.
level.roman_republic_1849.intro: November 1848. In Rome the pope's minister Pellegrino Rossi has been murdered, and there is unrest in the streets. Pius IX, until recently the idol of the liberals, flees in disguise to the fortress of Gaeta in the Kingdom of Naples. In February 1849 a Constituent Assembly elected by universal male suffrage proclaims the Roman Republic. It is led by a triumvirate headed by Giuseppe Mazzini; Giuseppe Garibaldi commands the volunteers and becomes the great hero of the defence.
level.roman_republic_1849.source: Constitution of the Roman Republic (3 July 1849); Giuseppe Garibaldi, «Memoirs»
level.roman_republic_1849.title: The Roman Republic
level.sardinia_1720.fact: In 1718 the Spanish landed in Sicily, but the Quadruple Alliance — Great Britain, France, Austria and the Netherlands — moved against them. The British fleet defeated the Spanish off Cape Passaro, the French invaded Spain, and in December 1719 Philip V dismissed Alberoni. Under the Treaty of The Hague of 1720 Emperor Charles VI received Sicily, and Victor Amadeus II received Sardinia and the title of King of Sardinia. The kingdom was governed from Turin, and the island itself long remained a poor periphery. A hundred and forty years later the «Kingdom of Sardinia» would become the core of a united Italy, but in 1720 no one was thinking of a united Italy: this was a dynastic deal among the great powers.
level.sardinia_1720.goal: Cardinal Alberoni's Spain tries to win back Sicily, four powers stop it — and Savoy trades Sicily for Sardinia along with a royal crown
level.sardinia_1720.hint: The exchange is decided at The Hague, not on the island. First Spain has to lose its gamble.
level.sardinia_1720.intro: 1718. After the War of the Spanish Succession, Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy became King of Sicily — but Madrid has not accepted it. Queen Elisabeth Farnese and her minister, Cardinal Giulio Alberoni, a gardener's son from Piacenza, dream of winning back Spain's Italian possessions. The Spanish fleet is already sailing for Palermo.
level.sardinia_1720.source: Treaty of The Hague (17 February 1720); Christopher Storrs, «War, Diplomacy and the Rise of Savoy, 1690–1720» (1999)
level.sardinia_1720.title: An Island for an Island
level.sicily_827.fact: Euphemius fled to Ifriqiya and asked the emir for help, promising to pay tribute. Ziyadat Allah consulted jurists at length over whether to break the peace with Byzantium, and in the end sent a fleet under the qadi Asad ibn al-Furat, a legal scholar of about seventy. In June 827 the army landed at Mazara and defeated the strategos Theodotus. Asad died of disease outside Syracuse, and in 828 Euphemius was killed by the Byzantines near Castrogiovanni. The conquest was slow: Palermo fell in 831, Syracuse in 878, Taormina in 902. Arab Sicily was neither a «disaster» nor a fairy-tale utopia: it meant two centuries of wars, taxes and the mingling of cultures, when the island came to know new irrigation systems, lemons, sugar cane and silk. The story of the nun is known only from late Byzantine sources.
level.sicily_827.goal: The Byzantine rebel Euphemius flees to Africa, the Aghlabid emir sends a fleet under an old qadi — and the army lands in Sicily
level.sicily_827.hint: Without a revolt there is no invitation, and a pardoned man has no one to call. Syracuse can't be taken head-on — they start from the western shore.
level.sicily_827.intro: 826. Sicily is a Byzantine province. The turmarch Euphemius, a fleet commander, falls into disgrace: according to a late chronicle, he faces having his nose cut off for abducting a nun. He raises a revolt and proclaims himself emperor, but cannot hold on. In Kairouan, the Aghlabid capital in North Africa, rules Emir Ziyadat Allah I.
level.sicily_827.source: Ibn al-Athir, «The Complete History»; al-Nuwayri; Theophanes Continuatus
level.sicily_827.title: Euphemius Calls the Aghlabids
level.statuto_1848.fact: In January 1848 Palermo rose up, and the King of Naples was the first to grant a constitution. Cavour, in his newspaper, demanded the same for Piedmont. On 4 March 1848 Charles Albert signed the Statute named after him: a two-chamber parliament, equality before the law, freedom of the press — but limited, with strong royal power and the vote for only a few. It was not modern democracy, yet the Statuto Albertino, unlike the other constitutions of 1848, was never revoked — and from 1861 it became the fundamental law of the Kingdom of Italy. Pius IX, meanwhile, soon disappointed the liberals: in April 1848 he refused to make war on Catholic Austria.
level.statuto_1848.goal: The new pope's reforms awaken hopes, Cavour and Balbo's newspaper demands a constitution — and Charles Albert signs the Statute that will become the fundamental law of united Italy
level.statuto_1848.hint: The press demands a constitution, but it is the king who grants it — if he doesn't give in to doubt.
level.statuto_1848.intro: 1846–1848. The new pope, Pius IX, begins with an amnesty for political prisoners and reforms — and all Italy cries «Viva Pio Nono!». In Turin, Count Camillo Cavour and the historian Cesare Balbo, moderate liberals, found the newspaper «Il Risorgimento» — «The Resurgence». King Charles Albert is cautious and devout: long ago he swore not to change the form of government.
level.statuto_1848.source: Statuto Albertino (4 March 1848); the newspaper «Il Risorgimento» (Turin, 1847–1848)
level.statuto_1848.title: The Statuto Albertino
level.theodoric_493.fact: The siege of Ravenna lasted almost three years. In February 493 Bishop John of Ravenna brokered an agreement: Odoacer and Theodoric would rule together. And on 15 March, ten days after entering Ravenna, Theodoric invited Odoacer to a feast at the palace of the Lauretum and killed him with his sword, reportedly saying: «There isn't even a bone in this wretch.» Odoacer's warriors and family were slaughtered. Theodoric ruled Italy for 33 years as King of the Goths and the emperor's representative: the Romans lived under Roman law, the Goths served in the army, and senators such as Cassiodorus and Boethius served at court. His mausoleum in Ravenna still stands. Justinian's Gothic War would begin only after his death.
level.theodoric_493.goal: Theodoric besieges Ravenna for three years, the bishop reconciles the rivals — and a few weeks later, at a feast, the King of the Goths kills Odoacer
level.theodoric_493.hint: A city in the marshes can't be taken by storm — only by hunger. And to invite a rival to a feast, you first have to make peace with him.
level.theodoric_493.intro: 489. Emperor Zeno rids himself of troublesome allies: he commissions the Ostrogothic king Theodoric to march on Italy and replace Odoacer there. The Goths and their families cross the Alps; Odoacer is beaten in the field and shuts himself up in Ravenna — an impregnable city among the marshes, supplied by sea.
level.theodoric_493.source: Anonymus Valesianus, Part II, 53–56; Jordanes, «Getica», 293–295; John of Antioch, fr. 214a
level.theodoric_493.title: The Feast at Ravenna
level.trent_1563.fact: The Council of Trent sat, with interruptions, from 1545 to 1563. In 1562–1563 the dispute over bishops' residence and papal authority nearly wrecked it; the Jesuit general Diego Laínez defended papal power, and the cardinal legate Giovanni Morone found a compromise in negotiations with the emperor and the kings. The pope's nephew, the young Cardinal Charles Borromeo, handled the correspondence and pressed for a conclusion. On 4 December 1563 the council closed. It confirmed doctrine, required bishops to reside in their dioceses, created seminaries, and ordered a catechism to be drawn up and the Missal and the Index of Forbidden Books to be revised (the papal Index had appeared in 1559, and the Roman Inquisition was established in 1542). Trent was not merely a «reaction»: it was a reform that shaped Catholicism for four hundred years; Borromeo later made Milan its model.
level.trent_1563.goal: A council that has dragged on for eighteen years is stuck on the dispute over bishops' authority — Laínez defends the pope's rights, the legates seek a compromise, Borromeo hurries Rome, and the Council of Trent closes
level.trent_1563.hint: Until the dispute over bishops is settled, the council's master won't convene the final session. Postponing is easy; finishing takes the pope's will.
level.trent_1563.intro: 1562, Trent — a city in the Alps on the border of Italy and the Empire. The Catholic Church convenes the council for the third time, to answer the Protestants and set its own house in order: the sale of indulgences, bishops who have not seen their dioceses for years, uneducated priests. The Spanish bishops demand recognition that the duty of residence is «by divine law», meaning the pope cannot dispense from it. The council has reached a deadlock.
level.trent_1563.source: Decrees of the Council of Trent (1545–1563); Paolo Sarpi, «History of the Council of Trent» (1619)
level.trent_1563.title: Trent Closes the Council
level.turin_1706.fact: The siege lasted almost four months. The citadel of Turin was riddled with underground galleries for countermines. On the night of 30 August French grenadiers broke into one of them; the sapper Pietro Micca, with no time to light the mine with a long fuse, lit a short one, brought down the gallery and was killed. On 7 September 1706 Eugene, having outmanoeuvred the French, attacked the besiegers together with the duke, and the French army fled, abandoning its artillery — France lost northern Italy for a long time. Under the Peace of Utrecht of 1713 Victor Amadeus received Sicily and a royal title. So little Savoy became a European power — the future core of Italian unification. Micca was later made a national symbol; his deed is documented, but the details have grown into legend.
level.turin_1706.goal: The Duke of Savoy goes over to France's enemies, the sapper Pietro Micca seals an underground passage against the French at the cost of his life — and Prince Eugene lifts the siege of Turin
level.turin_1706.hint: An ally is chosen before the siege, not during it. A city that has already been surrendered won't live to see help. Underground, it's the sapper who decides, not the marshal.
level.turin_1706.intro: 1706, the War of the Spanish Succession. Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy rules a small Alpine state between France and Austria. In 1703 he broke with Louis XIV and went over to the Grand Alliance. Now Marshal La Feuillade's French army is besieging his capital, Turin. Help is coming under the duke's cousin, Prince Eugene of Savoy, the finest general of the Austrian army.
level.turin_1706.source: Accounts of the 1706 siege of Turin; Eugene of Savoy, correspondence and military dispatches of 1706
level.turin_1706.title: Turin Holds
level.venice_1797.fact: On 1 May 1797 Bonaparte declared war on Venice. Senator Francesco Pesaro called for the lagoon to be defended, but Doge Ludovico Manin and most of the patricians feared destruction. On 12 May the Great Council — without a legal quorum, to the sound of gunfire — voted to hand power to a «provisional municipality». Manin, as tradition has it, took off his ducal cap and gave it to a servant: «Take it, I won't be needing it any more.» The French entered the city and carried the horses of St Mark's off to Paris. And on 17 October 1797 at Campo Formio, Bonaparte and the Austrian diplomat Count Cobenzl signed a peace: Austria received Venice, France received Belgium, and Lombardy remained in the Cisalpine Republic, dependent on France. Venetian democrats who had believed in «liberation» felt betrayed; Pesaro returned to the city as an Austrian commissioner.
level.venice_1797.goal: Under Bonaparte's threat the Great Council votes to end a thousand-year-old republic — and five months later Venice is handed to Austria
level.venice_1797.hint: Venice is not conquered — first it is made to abdicate. Only then can it be traded.
level.venice_1797.intro: Spring 1797. Bonaparte's army is crushing the Austrians in northern Italy. The neutral Republic of Venice — one of the oldest in Europe, more than a thousand years old — has neither an army nor allies. In Verona the townspeople have risen against the French (the «Veronese Easter»), and off the Lido a Venetian fort has fired on a French ship. Bonaparte declares: «I shall be an Attila to Venice.»
level.venice_1797.source: Treaty of Campo Formio (17 October 1797); minutes of the Great Council of Venice, 12 May 1797
level.venice_1797.title: The Last Doge
level.venice_1866.fact: On 8 April 1866 Italy and Prussia concluded an alliance. A few weeks before the war Austria secretly offered to cede Venetia in return for neutrality, but Italy stayed true to the treaty. On 24 June at Custoza the Italian army, divided between La Marmora and Cialdini, lost to the Austrians, and on 20 July the fleet was beaten off the island of Lissa. But on 3 July Prussia defeated Austria at Sadowa. Garibaldi won at Bezzecca and was already marching on Trento when he received the order to withdraw, and he answered with a single word: «Obbedisco» — «I obey». Under the Peace of Vienna Austria handed Venetia to Napoleon III, and he passed it to Italy; a plebiscite in October confirmed the annexation. Italy gained the region without winning a single major battle — and that remained a painful memory for a long time.
level.venice_1866.goal: Italy, allied with Prussia, loses to Austria at Custoza — and still gains Venetia, because its ally won the war
level.venice_1866.hint: Venetia is given for loyalty to the alliance, not for victories. Vienna offered a deal too — but it won't be handed to one who breaks the alliance.
level.venice_1866.intro: 1866. Italy is united, but Venetia is still under Austria. The Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck is preparing a war with Vienna for primacy in Germany and is looking for an ally. King Victor Emmanuel II can strike from the south. The army is commanded by General Alfonso La Marmora; Garibaldi leads the volunteers in the Alps.
level.venice_1866.source: Italo-Prussian treaty of alliance (8 April 1866); Peace of Vienna (3 October 1866)
level.venice_1866.title: Venetia without Victory
level.vienna_1815.fact: Under the decisions of the Congress of Vienna, Austria received the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia, and Habsburg relatives received Tuscany, Modena and Parma. The Kingdom of Sardinia of the House of Savoy recovered Piedmont and gained the former Republic of Genoa, although the Genoese asked for their independence to be restored.
